newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman party edges rival bloc in Zagreb election.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman party edges rival bloc in Zagreb election.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman's party beat a loose opposition bloc by half a percentage point in symbolically important elections for the city assembly in the Croatian capital of Zagreb, final official returns showed on Wednesday.

Preliminary returns from the April 13 vote put two allied centre-left parties ahead by a whisker but a final count reversed the order, awarding the ruling HDZ party 24 seats to its rivals' 23. A small moderate party won three.

The conservative nationalist HDZ, or Croatian Democratic Union, will need a coalition to regain a viable majority and hoped to attain it with one or two of the four other opposition parties, analysts said.
They said the HDZ, with 34.92 percent of the vote, would woo the Social Liberals (HSLS), with 10.5 percent. The HSLS was loosely aligned with Social Democrats (SDP), who polled 23.91.

But political observers see the HSLS as a wavering centrist party with at least as much in common with the HDZ as with the SDP, who as former communists ruled Croatia until defeated by Tudjman in 1990 elections.

Tudjman led Croatia in a war for independence from Yugoslavia in 1991. The HDZ has ruled as a quasi-monolithic state party since then despite a democratic constitution. But opposition parties have revived since 1995.

A seven-party bloc including the HSLS and SDP outpolled the HDZ in 1995 elections for the Zagreb assembly. But Tudjman used his presidential "national security" veto to block an opposition takeover of the mayoralty and imposed provisional rule that survived court challenges.
But Western diplomats said Tudjman could not afford to flout electoral principles again after Croatia's conditional admission in 1996 to the Council of Europe, antechamber to the European Union.

This time his HDZ narrowly defeated the combined Social Liberals and Social Democrats in the capital, which boasts a third of Croatia's 4.7 million population, half its industry and a powerful patronage machine.

Several factors boosted the HDZ, including widespread opposition disunity, signs of post-war reconstruction, HDZ domination of major media and Tudjman's "Father of the Nation" charisma, now heightened by his rebound from a bout with cancer.
The elections underlined hopes for a new era of peace in Croatia by including the country's last Serb enclave for the first time.

Former rebel Serbs in Eastern Slavonia/Baranja voted for municipal and regional assemblies on April 13-14, winning 11 of 29 districts in preparation for the enclave's reintegration with the rest of Croatia this summer.
In Zagreb, independent commentators said HDZ strategists saw important benefits in seeking a coalition with the HSLS.

Not only would it preclude a repeat of the 1995-96 impasse but also give the HDZ its first broad coalition of any import, helping make it look constructive and softening its image of arrogance, the weekly Nacional said.
The Liberals, for their part, would improve their political profile and gain experience in government before the next parliamentary elections in Croatia in 1999.
Presidential elections are due this summer. Tudjman, 75 in May, says he will run despite recent illness and is widely tipped to win easily over colourless potential challengers.
